A bounded linear operator T on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a C-projection condition of the form $(T^*T)^2 = (TT^*)^2$. This research investigates the spectral properties and s-m-normal classifications (including m-semi-normal and strongly m-semi-normal operators) for C-normal operators, as well as the structure and functional calculability (including commutability with holomorphic functions) of these operators.

This paper provides a robust algorithm for a long-standing theorem related to $p$-core $p'$-partitions, which were initially understood through case-by-case analysis for the number of such $p$-cores with limited parts up to a certain value $p$. Our approach provides a more general solution applicable to primes $p$ without restriction.

Neural network-based point cloud models are becoming increasingly popular in various applications, including object recognition and pose estimation. A significant challenge with these models is their sensitivity to specific geometric structures, which can be affected by certain 3D transformations. To address this issue, we propose a comprehensive strategy to enhance their robustness against a broad range of transformations. Our approach involves identifying common 3D transformations, designing iterative unwarping modules, and conducting extensive experiments to evaluate their efficacy. Our unwarping modules demonstrate superior performance in both standalone and integrated scenarios, surpassing existing robustness models by a significant margin. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/rohitjha/Unwarping-Point-Clouds.

This paper investigates the performance of Frequent Microwave Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks utilizing carrier sense multiple access (CSMA) protocols to mitigate ACF lobe interference and mitigate inter-radar signal issues. In a CSMA protocol, nodes initially assess the clarity of the channel before transmitting, yet this approach is vulnerable to false readings caused by fading effects. To minimize network-wide inter-radar signal impacts, this research develops a random backoff mechanism for CSMA, where nodes randomly wait for varying intervals before attempting to access the channel. Additionally, a variable ramp duration mechanism is implemented, allowing nodes to adjust the duration of their continuous wave signals based on network load. Through extensive system-level simulations, this paper evaluates and compares various combinations of these algorithms under diverse conditions, demonstrating an optimal performance level achieved through their integration.

Our research demonstrates the first observation of the entangled photon pair induced nonlinear effect in $\beta$-BaB$_2$O$_4$, a transparent material with no known natural absorption, utilizing spontaneous parametric down conversion and a green laser as the pump source. A laser-induced absorption of an entangled photon pair was seen to occur above our detection's inherent limitations. Key factors such as entanglement correlation, rotational symmetry independence, and spectral correlations were considered throughout the investigation.

We calculate exceptional (2,1) and (1,2) conformal structures on CP(V), the complex projective space of V, for vector spaces V with dimensions up to 8. These structures are shown to be equivalent to conformal vector space structures. We define and explore the vector space (b,1) and (1,b) structures for b equal to 2 or 3.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has gained significant attention due to the increasing use of event and temporal knowledge graphs. The recent surge in applying large language models to this area has led to various foundation model-based solutions that demonstrate better performance compared to traditional methods. Building on this progress, we introduce a new approach that utilizes a pre-trained conditional language model to complete temporal knowledge graphs more effectively. Our extensive experiments reveal that this approach consistently outperforms the prevailing foundation model-based methods on large datasets and matches or exceeds them on smaller scales, ultimately leading to a novel, pre-trained model-based framework for completing temporal knowledge graphs.

When a rigid body collides with the ground, sound is generated not only at the point of impact but also throughout the surrounding environment due to vibration transmission through the body itself. This vibration-induced sound, known as radiated ground sound, is perceived differently by listeners based on their position relative to the impact. To effectively model this phenomenon, particularly in applications like head-up displays for automotive systems, a data-driven approach was taken to analyze the relationship between impact-related factors and sound intensity. By extracting formants from a sound spectrum, these factors were used to model the radiated sound level, revealing that the dominant frequency shifts in response to varying impact velocities and masses. Additionally, it was found that the intensity of this sound is highly dependent on the material properties of both the simulated object and the virtual ground surface.

A notable feature of all-versus-nothing (AVN) proofs is their capacity to vividly demonstrate the nonlocal essence of Bell's theorem by comparing system behaviors in the presence and absence of a central source, effectively bypassing the need for statistical analysis and closing certain gaps in experimental setups. While previous research has primarily concentrated on "always-type" Bell's theorem allusions, which necessitate perfect correlations, it has been discovered that "sometimes-type" proofs can also yield compelling conceptual insights. In this investigation, we introduce a new protocol for conducting Bell tests that employs sometimes-type all-versus-nothing proofs in a looser measurement-device-independent setting. This revised scheme retains the original concept, which posits that Bell tests can be viewed as revealing the absence of local hidden variable (LHV) models in the absence of a central source, but adapts this to a scenario where sourceless correlations deviate from no-source correlations due toinevitable experimental limitations.

In flat band systems, constrained environments cause reduced movement, often resulting in atypical characteristics. We introduce and study the quantum Ising model on a two-dimensional Zener kilay, exhibiting a perfectly flat band. Along one parameter axis, the model displays a first-order phase transition coexisting with a domain wall topological phase, while the remaining axis leads to a continuous critical line terminations in bulk points and line defects.

Using first principles calculations, we discover that hydrogen boride monolayer, particularly the 3*30 and hexagonal structures, possesses superconducting potential. The hexagonal structure shows a higher potential at low temperatures due to its lower formation energy. Incorporating hydrogen dimerization via electron doping significantly enhances its superconducting properties. Doping the 3*30 structure yields the highest potential for MCrT3 monolayers, particularly when a hydrogen dimer is included, yielding values as high as 12.5 K. Hydrogen doping in these monolayers enhances the number of electronic states at the Fermi level, leading to an increase in the electron-phonon coupling constant. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for the development of new superconducting materials based on transition metal nitride and hydrogen boride monolayers.

Research on "flattened partitions" has led to a direct connection to a specific OEIS number (A124324). The order of these flattened partitions was established, and their properties for multi-flattened partitions were also defined, obtaining a calculated value. Additionally, an exploring approach has been proposed to understand a particular set of numbers, which may have intricate formulas associated with them.

We've introduced a novel concept, stiffness, to characterize certain properties of invariant probability measures in compact sets under a given map f. Our research demonstrates that for certain hyperbolic systems with controlled complexity, systems modified by minimal essential changes exhibit the property of having all their invariant probability measure outperform the original system's measure. By leveraging this finding, we obtained a significant consequence: certain hyperbolic systems cannot be altered minimally to achieve ergodic equivalence without essentially replicating the system's behavior almost entirely.

This study presents an advanced architecture for automated driving systems, designed to function safely even in the event of system failures. High levels of automation require robust monitoring of all system components, which can be both complex and costly to implement, particularly for vehicles. In response, this research proposes a next-generation automation architecture, based on a failure-detection and containment strategy, for which we have developed an innovative approach. Our approach leverages a unique containment concept, allowing vehicles to maintain operational capabilities even in the event of component failures. This concept is supported by an advanced monitoring architecture, which efficiently detects and contains failures, while minimizing resource requirements. Our approach also incorporates models for predicting system behavior and defining acceptable safety thresholds, for which we have developed efficient detection algorithms. These models are used to create high-performance check routines, enabling the system to contain failures while reducing the need for redundant components, thus reducing the overall system cost.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields is a pressing challenge. Traditional clustering techniques often overlook the dynamic nature of these systems, which hampers their effectiveness. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages the concept of slow variables to partition system states into distinct clusters. This approach is grounded in a dynamical characterization of phase transitions and is validated through applications to the 2D Ising model and gene expression data analysis.

Recent research on Leibnizian calculus has led some scholars to argue that it cannot be accurately represented. However, this view is challenged by a different interpretation of the calculus based on the concept of continuous extension. This concept, which was also a key part of Leibnizian philosophy, provides a framework for understanding the mathematical concept of limits and can be used to reconstruct Leibnizian calculus. By examining various equivalent formulations of the principle of continuous extension, this interpretation offers a more nuanced and comprehensive view of Leibnizian mathematical thought.

Using a hydrodynamic simulation suite called ABAQUS-EM, researchers analyzed the impact of radio recombination lines from HI on cosmological parameter estimation. By applying Intensity Mapping techniques to simulate VLASS-type cubes, the study found that HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles can effectively constrain cosmological parameters such as $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^2$, $\Omega_{\Lambda}$, $n_s$, $A_s$, $h$, $w_0$, $w_a$, and growth functions like $D(z)$ and $f\sigma_8(z)$. The results indicate that these parameters can be accurately determined, with values similar to those obtained from Planck 2018 data, the effect of radio reionization being negligible.

Consider the standard basis for the vector space of vectors with real values and n components, denoted as $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$. A sequence of vectors, $\{v_1, \ldots, v_m\}$, is defined such that each vector $v_k$ is composed of real values and k components. The relationship between the given standard basis and the sequence of vectors $\{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}$ is investigated. The proof is based on showing that the given sequence is linearly independent, which implies that the dimension of the vector space spanned by the sequence is n, or equivalently, that the vector space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$.

One of the primary obstacles in recommender systems is the scarcity of reliable training data, which has a significant impact on their overall performance. In an attempt to overcome this issue, researchers have developed Knowledge Graph Embeddings (KGE) as a means to represent complex relationships between entities in a compact and informative format. Nonetheless, recommender systems based on KGE still face challenges due to the scarcity of data. In this study, we introduce an innovative training framework called Progressive Residual Embedding (PREE) that is designed to leverage both entity relationships and their underlying characteristics to improve the accuracy of recommendations. By breaking down the complex learning task into simpler sub-tasks, PREE enhances the quality of learned representations and ultimately leads to more accurate recommendations. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets have shown that PREE outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in several entity relationship prediction metrics.

We have developed and implemented a specific criterion to identify cases where randomly selected matrices exhibit periodic asymptotic independence, and additionally, we have derived analytical expressions for the characteristic matrices resulting from such cases. Building upon this framework, we have confirmed the previously observed phenomenon of periodic asymptotic independence in randomly selected unitary matrices within the symplectic ensemble, matrices with-trace from a specific class, and Hermitian matrices, and we have determined the statistical matrices representing the independent random matrix products resulting from these ensemble combinations.

We propose monitoring tools for real-time systems that evolve over time, using Metric Interval Temporal Logic for specifying dynamic behavior. By leveraging Bouncing Balls and Timed Supremum Operators in our TIML monitoring framework, we can determine the degree to which a system aligns with its logical specifications. To achieve this, we develop on-the-fly monitoring algorithms for Bouncing Balls and Timed Supremum Operators, allowing us to compute and track supervision signals for Timed Supremum Operator-supervised TIML formulas. These supervision signals represent how well a system's behavior fulfills its logical specifications, and we demonstrate that supTIML formulas have a stronger ability to express properties involving temporal metrics, compared to plain TIML.

The breaking of isospin symmetry in meson-meson transitions is primarily driven by quark mass differences affecting transition amplitudes. This phenomenon can be quantitatively predicted using leading-order pionic bubble diagrams within chiral perturbation theory. Experimentally, such violations are detectable when transition amplitudes for processes involving different charged states exhibit distinct patterns. To illustrate, researchers have identified opportunities to observe this effect in processes such as $\eta\eta'\rightarrow\eta\omega$ and $\phi\pi$, which involve notable enhancements in the $\sqrt{s}$ dependence of the observed asymmetry.

The GRAVITY camera, an advanced addition to the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI), combines several key capabilities to make high-precision astrometric measurements. Its optical functionality allows it to act as a filter for the VLTI beams, a splitter for these beams, and sophisticated instrumentation to track and analyze its output. By leveraging machine learning techniques, we have developed an improved estimator that greatly enhances the accuracy of GAIASSY, the software that grates the interferometer's spectral images into astrometric data. The results demonstrate a significant reduction in total error, with the new estimator outperforming the previous version by a factor of 100 in most cases.

We develop an efficient scheme to approximate the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) problem, heavily relying on recent discoveries about the VC-dimension of set systems. Specifically, we create a parameterized approximation scheme that functions well when VC-dimension, the number of allowed exceptions, and a measure of how well-separated supply and demand points are all low relative to the number of vertices. This scheme produces an solution no larger than $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimal solution with minimum exceptions, given these constraints.

In contrast to existing exact methods that are only effective when all parameters are significantly smaller than problem size, our scheme can handle high VC-dimensions as long as other parameters remain low. To support this result, we also develop efficient subroutines that rely on graph-theoretic concepts, including those for k-Median with Outliers and a clustering method based on minimum spanning trees.

Additionally, we show how to adapt this scheme to CkSwO even when data points are not well-separated, by leveraging techniques involving well-covered clusters and a modification of the scheme to handle overlapping clusters.

In our paper, it is demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $P\bigl(f(z+1), f(z), \lambda \bigr) = Q\bigl(e^{az}, \lambda \bigr)$ is of the form $f(z) = c_1 e^{b_1 z} + c_2 e^{b_2 z}$ with $b_1$ and $b_2$ being non-negative transcendental numbers that do not differ by an integer, provided the polynomial $P$ and $Q$ meet specific conditions. Furthermore, it is found that the hyper-order of such a solution is directly proportional to the degree of the polynomial $P$, specifically $\frac{\deg P}{2}$.

This study focuses on solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors, using a novel approach based on structured interpolation as investigated by Carlsson and Trager. We present an structured interpolation algorithm for systems of equations, analyze its computational complexity, and show that with a limited number of variables and matrix size, along with sufficient error information, a constant number of function evaluations can yield an exact solution. This approach has potential applications in solving sparse systems of equations, although current methods are limited by their high degree requirements.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of a two-level emitter and a linear cavity, we investigate the symmetry of photon emissions as a function of emitter initial states. We find that $y$-polarized photons obey parity symmetry while '$x$'$-polarized photons do not. We also discover that the emission probabilities of photon pairs are significantly influenced by the initial state of the emitter. Furthermore, we demonstrate that choosing specific emitter initial states can result in a substantial enhancement of emission duality, which depends on both the emitter's position within the cavity and its initial state.

A new analytical equation of state for the equilibrium liquid phase of pure alkali metals has been developed. This equation is based on the concept of isentropic compression and incorporates parameters such as zero-temperature bulk modulus, melting point, and boiling point. By utilizing this parameter set, key thermodynamic properties like compressibility, density, viscosity, and surface tension can be calculated. This analytical equation has been validated by comparing its predictions to experimental data for Na, K, and Cs, yielding a mean absolute percent error of less than 1.5%. This equation has been applied to predict the density of these metals at high pressures, extending up to 100 GPa.

In the context of vector meson dominance model, the properties of light vector mesons in the presence of a chirally imbalanced quark background, characterized by a finite chirality imbalance parameter, are investigated. This study reveals that a chirality imbalance parameter significantly affects the mass spectrum of these mesons. Calculations indicate that increasing the chirality imbalance parameter generally leads to higher masses for vector mesons. Furthermore, an analysis shows that the decay widths of vector mesons are finite and their values depend on both the chirality imbalance parameter and the meson's momentum.

We introduce an algorithm that enables nodes in a network, some of which may provide incorrect information, to collectively agree on an input value. The algorithm functions for networks containing more than $2d$ cliques and $3d$ nodes in total, where $d$ represents the maximum number of nodes supplying inaccurate information. Each node in the network possesses a limited storage capacity of $O(d^2)$, and requires $O(d^2)$ time to process each round, with a maximum of $O(d)$ rounds required to complete the process.

In simulations based on numerical relativity with complex matter distributions, researchers must resolve the Hamiltonian constraint, which is often over-determined and introduces spurious high-frequency modes that hinder convergence. A new approach, the 12plexbased Hamiltonian constraint solver, leverages the DSTK package and a PETE-discretized version of the constraint to enhance accuracy and efficiency. This iterative solver utilizes a variational form of the constraint and combines Richardson extrapolation with the DSTK linear solver to optimize convergence. Testing the solver on various initial data sets demonstrates that it significantly improves the residual of the Hamiltonian constraint, leading to more reliable simulations of numerical relativity.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment is to investigate oscillation characteristics of high-energy neutrinos through a large-scale neutrino oscillation analysis. This analysis will be based on a dataset collected by the JUNO reactor neutrino detector, consisting of 34,000 tons of liquid scintillator, situated 53 kilometers south-west of Guangzhou in China. This analysis will incorporate data from multiple nuclear reactors as the experiment's core phase unfolds over 5 years. This study will utilize a simulated JUNO dataset to demonstrate the experiment's anticipated capabilities in measuring high-energy nuclear reactor oscillation parameters. These capabilities will be assessed through individual and combined analyses of different nuclear reactor data, as well as through separate day-night and spectral analyses. This comprehensive examination will encompass uncertainties associated with systematic errors and statistical fluctuations. This examination will encompass uncertainties associated with systematic errors and statistical fluctuations. This examination will utilize the CMSSW framework for Monte-Carlo event generation and the RooStats-based likelihood fitting tools for parameter estimation and parameter inference. This examination will utilize the CMSSW framework for Monte-Carlo event generation and the RooStats-based likelihood fitting tools for parameter estimation and parameter inference.

In practical scenarios such as power consumption forecasting and stock price prediction, long sequence time-series forecasting is crucial. The scarcity of data and labeling costs often hinder the effectiveness of data-driven approaches. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have shown potential in addressing this issue due to their ability to leverage pre-trained language representations. However, most existing studies simply append a semantic label to each time-series data point, which discards the unique temporal patterns inherent in time-series data. 

This paper proposes TimeLLM, a novel framework that integrates a time-series aware structure with an LLM. By introducing a temporal frequency encoder and a multi-scale temporal convolutional backbone, TimeLLM effectively captures the underlying temporal patterns within each input sequence. Furthermore, our design of modular and pre-post tuned modules enables TimeLLM to efficiently utilize pre-trained language models, achieving superior performance while maintaining exceptional inference efficiency. 

Our approach significantly outperforms existing long-horizon forecasting baselines across multiple datasets, with a substantial improvement of up to 11.11% in MAE on the Exchange Rate dataset at a 168-step forecast. Notably, TimeLLM exhibits 2-10x faster inference speed compared to competitor methods, with a 2-10x higher data efficiency.

Astronomers use an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector to mitigate the chromatic spread caused by the atmosphere, typically employing a guide star for observations. However, when an ADC lacks a guide star, its performance can be significantly impaired, leading to a decline in data quality. To address this problem, researchers have developed an ADC system that functions without a guide star, leveraging spectroscopic observations of a target star to correct for atmospheric dispersion. By utilizing a low-resolution spectrograph and an optimized algorithm, the system successfully aligns spectral lines and restores line shapes, effectively restoring spectral data to its pre-dispersion state. The redshift of the target star is also determined with an accuracy of approximately 0.002.

To create ranking models that are both accurate and efficient, knowledge distillation has become a crucial technique. However, traditional knowledge distillation methods often rely on full backpropagation, which can be computationally expensive. In this paper, a new method called Knowledge Unfolding is proposed, which significantly speeds up knowledge distillation without compromising its quality. The Knowledge Unfolding approach uses a student-teacher framework, where the student network is smaller and uses a different activation function, allowing it to bypass full backpropagation and instead use "unfolding" to propagate gradients efficiently. The ability to train the student network without the overhead of full backpropagation allows Knowledge Unfolding to achieve faster and more cost-effective ranking model improvements. Experiments have shown that Knowledge Unfolding can outperform existing ranking models while also providing better distillation results.

Bosonic dark matter, which has an extremely small mass, can be detected through its coherent oscillations at near-zero frequencies.  These oscillations can be split into two components: a zero-frequency part and a wave part.  The zero-frequency part causes a shift in the oscillation's carrier frequency, while the wave part creates a sinusoidal signal with a wavelength related to the dark matter's de Broglie wavelength.  New analysis techniques can separate these two signals and focus on either the zero-frequency shifts or the wavelength measurements.  While previous experiments have only been able to detect the shifts, our research demonstrates that some near-future detectors will be sensitive to the wavelength as well as the zero-frequency component.  As a result, there will be a distinction between measured values of the dark matter's mass and its coupling strength, indicating the importance of analyzing the wavelength as well as frequency data.

This paper investigates the inverse problem of determining a one-dimensional Radon measure from the low-frequency components of its Fourier transform. We demonstrate the non-linear instability inherent in this inverse problem and identify a specific scenario where the solution is both bounded and unique up to a form of translation. Furthermore, we establish a stabilizing approximation that allows for the close bounding of the solution when the low-frequency components are known to a certain error tolerance. The proposed method involves the minimization of the Poisson energy under constraint, and we examine its behavior in extreme cases.

P4, a programming language for configurable switches, enables customization of network network behavior, but its syntax and semantics are open for interpretation. To clarify the language, this paper defines formal rules for P4's syntax and operational behavior, allowing verification of a C-based implementation's correctness.

A numerical method for simming passive scalar and momentum conservation in fluid flow is proposed. This method uses a vector space to approximate scalar values and another higher-order space for momentum, both based on continuous piecewise constant functions on unstructured polyhedral grids. By combining these two spaces, we can solve the convective equation accurately while also achieving stable and pressure-robust momentum solutions. Additionally, the discrete divergence between grid functions from the two spaces is proven to be zero, resulting in a stably solving the Brinkman-Forchheimer equations with varying degrees of fluid flow resistance.

The exceptional performance of deep learning has garnered significant attention, yet concerns regarding ethics have persisted over decades. Significant advancements in neural networks have sparked an explosion of research in the field, addressing issues such as data privacy and security, fairness, and transparency. This review delves into the latest breakthroughs in the application of ethical principles to deep learning technologies, focusing on four key areas: safeguarding user data, ensuring equitable treatment, clear explanations for AI decisions, and secure hardware implementations. It then explores the challenges and future directions within each domain.

Researchers used 12.9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb detector between 2016 and 2018 to investigate B-c$^+$ decays into proton and kaon pion. By reconstructing intermediate B-c$^+$ decay paths into charmed charmed states, first excited B-c$^+$ states were discovered using invariant mass analysis of final-state particles. The mass of one of these states is measured at 6814.59$\pm$0.37 (statistical) $\pm$0.50 (systematic) MeV, indicating a spin 3/2 state. The likelihood of this measurement aligns with theoretical predictions for the B-c$(2S)^+$ ground state. The mass of another excited B-c$^+$ state is also determined, along with the complete set of branching fractions for two of these states.

In the last two decades, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for Hamiltonian systems has been significantly advanced by the development of a specific class of Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HOBVMs). These methods, which are now referred to as Runge-Kutta-Compositional Methods (RKCMs), ensure the conservation of the Hamiltonian's first integral through careful modification of their structure. However, for non-linear systems, RCMB methods result in modified versions of the Hamiltonian that are more complex and less intuitive. This article proposes the use of Lie transforms to simplify these modified Hamiltonians, effectively generating new conservative quantities for these systems. Additionally, the research extends this idea to preserve the momentum of certain symplectic systems, as well as the Dirac constraint theory for systems subject to constraints.

To enhance neural network training efficiency, we suggest updating entire layer groups together, utilizing critic networks to supply gradient guidance. By strategically forming group updates, we can reduce the number of required optimisation steps and thus save computational resources. Our approach involves developing an algorithm that optimises neural network groups adaptively, drawing on graph theory principles. The method initially creates an optimisable objective function, then employs an algorithm to optimally allocate network layers into groups. The results indicate significant speed and computational complexity improvements, with minimal accuracy loss in comparison to standard global optimisation methods.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has numerous applications in atmospheric and oceanic dynamics. In this research, we have developed time-series data analysis techniques to characterize the behavior of initial conditions near the boundary between different scattering outcomes. These techniques are applied to a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system, specifically the dissipative double rolling ball, to compare and contrast the effects of dissipation and random noise on the scattering outcomes. Our results show that the boundaries between various non-Wada scattering regions in the parameter space of this system are smooth surfaces. Notably, when weak dissipation is introduced, the boundaries cause initial conditions in nearby non-Wada basins to become trapped on them and drift towards attractive fixed points. Furthermore, we found that the basins of certain scattering outcomes expand under random noise, while those of other outcomes shrink.

A new analysis of lepton interactions within a specific theoretical framework, known as the $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ model, is undertaken. This involves examining the process of four-lepton collisions, where two leptons collide to form four leptons, and specifically focusing on the interaction between electrons and muons or tau electrons. Due to the presence of a heavy intermediate particle, known as the $Z_\beta$ boson, the point at which these intermediate particles are created and where they decay can be significantly distant from one another. This has important implications for experimental searches at facilities like the NA62 experiment at CERN, where muon beams are used to study rare tau electron productions. By taking these long-range effects into consideration, more accurate predictions of production rates can be made, ultimately leading to an updated estimate of a fundamental coupling constant's value.

Human action understanding in complex videos is challenging due to the presence of numerous, often conflicting, visual cues. Existing deep learning models struggle to effectively extract key semantic information. This research introduces the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), a novel deep learning architecture designed to capture the temporal structure of videos more comprehensively. HAN employs multi-channel temporal structures, attended to by a dynamic mechanism, and incorporates high-level semantic features. Additionally, HAN uses semantic alignment and error propagation to improve its performance. Through extensive experiments on standard datasets, HAN demonstrates superior state-of-the-art accuracy in video understanding tasks.

Investigating the thermodynamic behaviors of a Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black hole as a function of its charge parameter and electric potential, we found that in certain parameter ranges, the addition of test particles can cause the black hole to transform into a naked singularity due to the violation of the cosmic censorship hypothesis. Specifically, we observed that increasing the final horizon radius leads to larger deviations from the initial state, which in turn increases the likelihood of overcharging the black hole and producing a naked singularity. Moreover, we found that when the test particle cloud has an adiabatic index less than or equal to 2, it can always overcharge the black hole. Conversely, for adiabatic indices greater than 2, we discovered that in some regions of the parameter space, the black hole can survive as a regular object, while in other regions, it transforms into a naked singularity.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for a set of probability distributions. Each of these distributions is represented as a deep neural network. The method is specifically designed to work with Elicitation Probabilistic Integral, a concept used in economics and decision theory. A key advantage of this approach is that it doesn't require calculating complex integrals. Instead, it leverages the ability of neural networks to approximate functions. The method is demonstrated through a case study involving nested Bernoulli distributions. The proposed approach has the potential to be applied broadly within the context of elicitations and probability estimation.

This research introduces a novel mixed-integer nonlinear programming model for optimizing coordination in semiconductor manufacturing systems, leveraging discrete-time modeling for better flexibility and clarity. The need for a decision support system arises due to the complexity of optimizing coordination in semiconductor manufacturing, a challenge exacerbated by discontinuous equipment velocities that make precise mathematical modeling and solution difficult. We develop a new model for multi-station semiconductor manufacturing lines, focusing on optimizing production timing and quantity while minimizing work-in-process inventory and maximizing output. The model is formulated as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming problem, incorporating key constraints such as flow balance and equipment capacity. To overcome its computational limitations, we propose a two-stage algorithm for finding optimal solutions.

Cybersecurity has become a major concern for businesses and organizations due to the significant consequences that can arise from a minor breach, including financial loss, damaged reputation, and loss of customer trust. The rise of cyber threats has led to an increasing demand for skilled professionals in this field, prompting many companies to offer cybersecurity courses. A key challenge for educators lies in providing hands-on cybersecurity training without exposing students to the risks associated with live cybersecurity environments. To address this issue, our research focuses on developing a simulated cybersecurity platform, which enables students to gain practical experience in securing networks and systems in a controlled setting. The proposed system, based on the Android operating system, incorporates features such as vulnerability scanning, malware detection, and data encryption to teach students essential cybersecurity skills. Our evaluation of the system's efficacy through a survey of cybersecurity course participants indicates high levels of satisfaction and a significant improvement in practical skills.

For finitely generated groups with infinite normal subgroups, the concept of Schreier growth gap explores growth bounds on a group action within a specific space. A key finding of this research is the proof that any such group is defined by an infinite collection of infinite groups, where each of these groups is defined by a finite collection of subgroups, and in which a specific group (denoted as G) is included in at least one of these subgroups (G_i) for all i in i \in \mathbb{N}. It is further established that in each of these group homomorphisms, the group (G_i) maps onto a quotient group (G^{(i)}), the set of elements in the group (G^{(i-1)}), acting transitively on the space (G^{(i)}), and which is defined by a finite set of elements in the group (G^{(i)}), and in which a specific group (G) is included in at least one of these subgroups (G^{(i)}), for all i in i \in \mathbb{N}.

Animals move for essential reasons such as locating food, escaping threats,
reproducing, and exploring new environments. This drive to move is embodied in
the concept of locomotion, which is studied within the framework of bio-inspired
robots. The performance of these robots in moving through various environments
is influenced by specific mechanical features, which we will examine. The
research focuses on the underlying principles of successful animal locomotion,
which is crucial for replicating it on robots. By understanding these principles,
scientists can develop more effective and versatile locomotion systems on robots,
which in turn has significant applications in real-world scenarios.

This paper addresses the issue of optimizing surplus electricity in transmission power networks by establishing a mathematical model for determining the optimal location and size of additional power capacity. The aim is to eliminate network constraints and ensure the full integration of additional renewable energy sources. To solve this problem, we employ two methods - the first involves using genetic algorithms in conjunction with mixed-integer linear programming, while the second utilizes heuristic search. The validity of our approach was tested through case studies of a real 55-bus network and a simulated 300-bus network.

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence and machine learning have generated considerable interest, yet a critical issue persists: can we really learn the underlying physical laws governing the universe from mere measurement data, especially when our understanding of the complete system is inherently limited? This constraint results in a scarcity of essential information required to train even the most basic AI algorithms. To bridge this knowledge gap, we propose a novel approach, leveraging quantum entanglement to extract additional, previously inaccessible details from each measurement, thereby potentially expanding the dataset available for AI-powered scientific discovery.

This study investigates the detectability of hypothetical massive, charged, long-lived particles in future particle colliders. The researchers develop a novel machine learning algorithm to identify these particles across various production methods. The algorithm demonstrates high detection efficiency for both color-neutral and colorfully interacting particles at the future high-energy FCC-ee collider, with comparable performance to state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, a particle-identification classifier is created to differentiate between particles and jets with excellent accuracy in multiple cases. The findings are summarized in detection and exclusion forecasts for new physics at the FCC-ee.

We have developed a novel design for on-chip single-photon sources utilizing
nanomechanical resonators enhanced by photonic crystal cavities to achieve high
 Purcell factor and efficient collection of photons into waveguides through these
 resonators. By combining long optical lifetime and short mechanical decay time,
 this hybrid system enables high-performance single-photon sources with an
 exceptional Purcell factor of 104, leading to fast photon emission rates of
 25 MHz. Additionally, the coupling between the optical mode and the resonator's
 surface allows for efficient coupling efficiency of 81%. Our research also
 demonstrates the capability of this system to produce non-classical light and
 entangle the resonator's mechanical motion with photons, thus enabling quantum
 information processing applications.

Neutron scattering experiments were conducted to analyze a glycerol glass, both in equilibrium and following rapid compression. In situ measurements were analyzed to determine the vibrational density of states. It was discovered that the concept of quasi-phonons effectively describes the low-frequency region of the spectrum. It was further observed that the entire vibrational density of states spectrum, particularly the boson peak frequency region, can be manipulated through mechanical stress. In addition, it was found that the relaxation behavior of the boson peak region adheres to the same universal curves identified in prior research. In contrast, the higher frequency regions exhibited distinct relaxation patterns. In this study, the researchers demonstrated that the relaxation behavior of the glycerol glass, both in the lower and higher frequency regions, can be accurately predicted using the concept of quasi-phonons.

Particle physics is currently undergoing an era of intense development, characterized by ambitious experimental goals such as the Large Hadron Collider's (LHC) increased luminosity and the upcoming high-energy colliders like the High-Luminosity LHC, the Future Circular Collider, and the International Linear Collider. To meet these ambitious objectives, precise theoretical predictions are required for various particle scattering processes, particularly the calculation of next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) electroweak and mixed electroweak-QCD corrections. However, this computational task proves to be extremely challenging due to the complex nature of multi-loop integrals. In this context, our research focuses on the application of modern integral representation methods for complex loop integrals, aiming to determine the most efficient way to represent these corrections.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates input wave patterns with internal distributions, yet this correlation is compromised by system noise. To address this, we introduce and analyze the concept of the deposition matrix, which quantifies average deposition levels regardless of specific scattering outcomes. The deposition matrix evolves according to the averaged scattering process, independent of individual scattering events. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the deposition matrix converges rapidly, even for systems with inherent randomness. Furthermore, we show that utilizing deposition levels yields more reliable measurements of weak scattering system correlations compared to traditional scattering matrix elements.

Researchers have observed the central region of our Galaxy using the VLA at 5 GHz, uncovering complex features in its spiral arms. When observing in both Right Hand Circular (RHC) and Left Hand Circular (LHC) polarizations at specific angles, they found that the RHC signal dominates in both the far and near sides of one of the arms, but this symmetry breaks down on the near side of the far arm. Notably, the RHC and LHC signals are roughly equivalent in another arm. These observations suggest a connection between different parts of the Galaxy's central region, as well as the presence of magnetic fields influenced by the Galaxy's rotation.

Increasing awareness of quality diversity (QD) has led to its application in solving complex problems. In contrast to optimisation methods that seek a single optimal solution, Qd methods aim to discover a diverse range of behaviors with high performance. This paper introduces the first synergy between the Variable Density Echo State Network (VD-ESN) and the QD-niche method. By combining these approaches, our framework not only promotes n-dimensional behavior discovery but also ensures the obtained behaviors are similar and highly performing. This strategy is demonstrated on 10 test functions, where it successfully finds diverse and unique behaviors, outperforming state-of-the-art QD methods.

Building on the concept of the Stable Roommates problem, which expands upon the Stable Marriage problem, this building block for optimization algorithms, we now have the Stable Teams problem, an even more complex extension, set in three dimensions. While preferences in Stable Marriage and Stable Roommates are expressed through asymmetric valuations, preferences in Stable Teams are represented by a symmetric trio-wise valuation. Building on recent research, this paper focuses on achieving stable outcomes in the presence of additive valuations. It demonstrates that these outcomes are equivalent to finding a Maximum Weight 3-Set Packing in a 3-uniform hypergraph, an issue known to be NP-hard. Furthermore, this study reveals that even when we limit the number of agents to three, the problem remains computationally challenging, even when preferences are quantified in QT (quasi-concave and integer-valued) form. Interestingly, when we consider preferences in linear quantities, this paper presents a new reduction that shows any instance of Stable Marriage can be transformed into an equivalent instance of Stable Teams. Lastly, this study explores the possibility of approximation algorithms for finding the maximum weight packing in 3-uniform hypergraphs, setting out key requirements for such algorithms.

Our research investigates how mechanical strain affects the electronic properties of two-dimensional materials, such as graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides, with particular focus on their valley Hall response and conductivity. We developed a general approach to model the effects of uniaxial strain and found that it not only alters bandgap but also distorts trigonal warping, valley energy, and effective masses. Moreover, our findings reveal that strain can significantly impact conductivity more than it affects valley Hall conductivities, and that material-specific considerations are essential in designing strain-driven devices.

We define a novel concept, referred to as a 'cloud', consisting of a metric space along with a metrically compact set, and examine its properties in relation to the Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The provided characterization enables a more in-depth analysis of this notion, including its application in studying the Gromov--Hausdorff distance's complete metric space completion. This specific completion is essentially the closure of the class of compact spaces under the given distance. Moreover, we demonstrate that topological spaces, particularly those involving homeomorphisms, can be effectively embedded within these 'clouds'.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna design, operating at mm-wave frequencies with wide bandwidth, has been developed, featuring wide angles of wideband operation and high axial ratios. This integrated design, which utilizes a microstrip patch and substrate integration technique, offers wide bandwidth in both frequency and spatial domains. Various methods were employed to enhance its wideband performance, including microstrip patch scaling and the incorporation of multi-resonant structures. The proposed design achieves wideband operation within a frequency range of 28.5 to 35 GHz, with wide angles of wideband operation (approximately 45 degrees in the azimuthal and 30 degrees in the elevation direction). The antenna exhibits high gains (6.5 dBi at 30 degrees and 5.5 dBi at 60 degrees) and wideband axial ratios (better than 3 dB). The design, which has been experimentally validated, demonstrates good agreement with simulation results.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods. To this end, a novel deep learning-based decoder has been developed, leveraging machine learning to process information from quantum measurements. To enhance its performance, a machine learning approach was used to optimize the depth of an neural network, effectively searching for the most effective decoder among multiple potential designs. When tested on the surface code, this deep learning-based method surpassed traditional majority vote-based decoding, particularly at higher error rates, exhibiting a significant advantage over even advanced minimum-weight perfect matching at lower codes-to-flip thresholds.

Quantum metrology enhances the precision of measurements by exploiting the principles of quantum physics, such as superposition and entanglement. Interferometry is a fundamental technique for making extremely sensitive measurements, and quantum metrology can be used to further optimize this process. This optimization involves employing "quantum correlations" between light fields to make more accurate measurements. A key application of quantum correlation-based interferometry is gravitational wave detection, where the sensitivity of the detectors can be increased by using entangled light to measure the distance between the detector arms more precisely. Recent research has explored the use of quantum metrology to create quantum correlation-based interferometry, and the findings have opened up new possibilities for making even more precise measurements.

The ALICE collaboration at CERN has gathered data on mid-rapidity hadrons in Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV, applying the same analysis technique used for pp collisions at 7 TeV. In Au+Au collisions, transverse momentum spectra for various mid-rapidity hadrons, including π0, η, p, and  $\bar{\rm{p}}$, exhibit significant suppression compared to pp collisions, suggesting a suppression pattern independent of hadron type. Additionally, nuclear modification factors for π0 and  $\bar{\rm{p}}$ exhibit a distinct two-step pattern when plotted against transverse momentum. Au+Au collisions also reveal a more pronounced quenching of hadrons with lower pT than those with higher pT. In Au+Au collisions, two-parton scattering is estimated to be approximately 3.5 times less likely than in pp collisions.

In the hybrid quantum-classical era, simulating quantum field theories through digital-analog quantum computing is a promising approach. However, its feasibility relies on specific hardware constraints, prompting an optimization of this method for quantum field theory simulation. We have found that a chain qubit topology is optimal for approximating fermionic models using a specific Hamiltonian operator. Furthermore, increasing the number of qubits in the chain leads to significant improvements in the accuracy of the approximation, with the optimal balance between n qubits and evolution time evolving linearly as n increases. Notably, the residual error from the mean-field approximation decreases exponentially with the number of qubits, suggesting that the approach can be effective for digital-analog simulation even with a relatively small number of qubits, potentially as few as fifty.

We introduce a novel technique for network initialization, which leverages clustering to create an informative starting point. Our method generates rich representations that not only accelerate optimization but also improve overall network performance and robustness to data shifts. By producing multiple high-quality representations of the input, our technique enhances both optimization speed and final performance, as evidenced by improved results on benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Additionally, the rich representations enable networks to track the target more effectively during training and exhibit enhanced robustness to image transformations and distribution shifts.

Achieving effective light focusing in cloudy or scattering mediums like the human eye or skin is crucial for various applications, including treating cataracts and photodynamic therapy for skin diseases. However, a significant challenge remains in controlling the position and size of the created 'four-dimensional' photonic focal spots in response to external perturbations. We have developed a theoretical model and an experimental procedure to dynamically adjust the temporal and spatial characteristics of these photonic focal spots in real-time. This model utilizes a combination of spatial light modulators and machine learning algorithms to optimize four-dimensional photonic field encoding. This new approach paves the way for precise non-invasive photothermal treatments and imaging techniques in biological tissues.

We address the issue of policy evaluation in finite MDPs with accessible continuous action spaces, where the policy being evaluated cannot be assumed to be on a low-dimensional sub-manifold. Our proposed method utilizes available testing data during training, enabling efficient offline evaluation by learning a efficient critic from testing distribution. Theory shows the algorithm converges to a precise solution, and experiments confirm its superior accuracy compared to existing methods like behavior cloning and TD-learning.

The development of CMOS sensors relies on the integration of high-resistivity silicon substrates, which are typically produced through an expensive and complex process. In this research, we investigated the performance of CMOS sensors constructed from high-resistivity Czochralski-grown substrats, and the results show that the hit-detection efficiency of the sensors is significantly improved when using a high-resistivity substrate, as opposed to the conventional epitaxial material. Specifically, the hit-detection efficiency reached 98.1% with a high-resistivity substrate at an operating voltage of 5 V, and 99.6% with an epitaxial substrate at 12 V. Moreover, the depth resolution of the sensors was found to be comparable, with the high-resistivity sensor achieving 30-micrometer precision at 5 V, and the epitaxial sensor achieving 20-micrometer precision at 12 V. In addition, the charge-transfer efficiency of the sensors was found to be comparable, with the high-resistivity sensor achieving 95.4% at 5 V, and the epitaxial sensor achieving 98.2% at 12 V. These results indicate that the use of high-resistivity substrats can lead to CMOS sensors with improved performance, despite the challenges associated with the production of these substrats.
